subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: The area of the North Village District is in need of your help. We would like to have the setback behind our houses changed from 50 feet to 100 feet. The additional 50 feet added on to this is NOT a lot of space. But it is enough that it would help us to be able to keep some semblance of a neighborhood. Jason and Ryan said in their letter to you that they applaud us for trying to preserve our neighborhood. However, they aren’t willing to budge on this issue. They think that the 50 foot setback is good enough. But, do you realize that they are not saying that nothing will be built in that 50 foot setback? They are saying that something that is 35 feet tall, could be built in that first 50 feet. The high density housing plan that is suppose to be kept on State Street and help to build up State Street, is not going to be on State Street at all. They are saying that it is going to start right at our back fences starting at 35 feet and then building up as it gets farther away. We are not against the North Village District being built. We realize that it is going to happen, and it could improve the city. However, we are asking you to work with us. We are asking you to help us preserve our neighborhoods just a little bit. Just adding an extra 50 feet to the setback behind the houses would help that. Even adding just an additional 25 feet to make it a 75 foot buffer would help us to preserve our neighborhood just a little more and keep the building height smaller near our fence lines. Having that little bit more space where something huge could not be so close to the houses would be the best thing in preserving a neighborhood. And that is what the State Street Master Plan was all about. It was created to help preserve neighborhoods and create more living space. But that is not what is happening right now. Plans are to build high density housing right next to residential. Right at the fence line to houses. There isn’t anything that is being put on State Street. I ask you, if this was being built right next to your houses, wouldn’t you want to have a little bit more of a buffer between it and you? Making the buffer 75-100 feet would guarantee that the building step up would be a little bit farther away from the homes. It would mean that we wouldn’t have a large structure right next to our backyards. It would mean that the 35 foot tall structure could still be able to be built there, but it would continue another 25-50 feet than is already planned. Think about it. 25-50 feet more. The size of one living room. That is the distance that we are asking for the height limits to be continued. Please help us add just a little bit more of a buffer to help us preserve our neighborhood. Please help us keep the original statement of using the State Street Master Plan to help preserve our neighborhoods true.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I have seen Phase 2 of the High-Density High Rise Housing Project that again affects 400 West in North Orem. This second project is a space from me, but Phase 1 is directly across the street from my residence. I do not understand the big rush to implement these housing projects, especially when they ‘bulldoze’ forward and ignore residents’ concerns. I have lived in an area, before I moved to Orem, where a high-density housing project was built directly behind my house. There was no buffer zone; the complex was literally six feet from my back fence. I used to be able to go into my backyard that was fenced, but with this housing project, I lost my privacy because people just looked out their window into my backyard. This Phase 2 project I see as a repeat of what I endured until I finally just had to sell my home where my family lived for thirty years because of this problem. If Orem City is going to continue to encourage high- density housing in residential areas, then it needs to create a buffer zone of 75 to 100 feet from adjacent home property lines. Many people have backyard patios, play areas for their families. High-rise housing robs them of their privacy, their enjoyment of an afternoon sunset. If these projects loom over residences, then in my opinion, they should be lower height as they near residential neighborhoods and houses. I watch traffic every morning come down 400 West to 1600 North. There are mornings when cars are backed up nearly to 2000 North. Phase 1 and 2 will inundate the area with traffic creating dangerous situations for families with children, pets, and just residents trying to gain access to the road in front of their homes. The speed limit on 400 West is 25 mph; I see cars exceed that limit all the time. Finally, there needs to be a 50 foot setback from homes that is nonstructural. Progress is a fact of life; I understand that; however, as a resident of Orem for thirty years, I should have the right to maintain my quality of living. I want to protect my home and continue the safety of my neighborhood. Increasing the ‘buffer zones’ and moving traffic access to State Street is one way of keeping a ‘good neighbor’ status between the city and its residents. Charles Tanner This is another silly problem to have placed in this area! It’s way too close to State st. And the quick light at 400 w. Just ridiculous to even have a meeting about it! Too much traffic on 1600 no. A very dangerous intersection already! To contend with!! I never wanted a left turn on 400 w the last time it was changed. Don’t slow !!!

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: Thank you, again, for taking the time to give attention to the North Village District and some of its challenges and concerns. Hopefully, you have had the opportunity to review the residents’ proposal and driving tour emailed to you earlier. Our hope is that this proposal and the real-life, visual examples of current setbacks has clarified the issue at hand, that residential homes need more protection and buffer from larger development in our area. The Planning Commission’s 50-foot setback proposal was tabled to further understand setbacks and the residents’ request to increase the setback to 100 feet. This 100-foot request is not as restricting as it appears. Rather, it gives guideline and direction to how property can be used – parking or the required 20% open space (Code of Ordinances 22-24-5-12), as well as providing an adequate buffer for adjacent residential property. The residents’ proposal includes a 50-foot “non-structure” area that can be addressed later. The main focus is the issue at hand - to increase the 50-foot setback to 100 feet, or a compromise of 75 feet, which hopefully the City Council will consider. This increased setback would still allow buildings of up to 35’ to be built within the first 100 feet (or 75-foot compromise), providing the necessary buffer that has not been achieved through zoning. Zoning in the North Village District uses the Edge Zone (NVD-E) as a transition from larger, commercial property to adjacent residential property. Being a transition zone, the Edge Zone should have a maximum height restriction to “feather” back from commercial and high-density housing, which is does not. Since Edge Zones do not have maximum height restrictions and allow high-density housing, an adequate buffer or setback is even more important. Increasing the proposed setback from 50 feet to 75, or even 100 feet, would provide a better buffer for these residential homes that abut Edge Zones.Increasing the already proposed 50-foot setback to 100, or even 75, would provide a more appropriate buffer in areas where Edge Zones abut residential. Again, this buffer area is not “dead space” but an area where structures can be up to 35 feet and where the required open space or parking could be directed. The North Village District is a narrow district with unique challenges. We hope the City Council will improve the Master Plan to accommodate the specific needs of this district. Thank you for taking the time to consider the residents in the North Village District. Residents would prefer the 100 foot setback - which still allows a 35 foot tall building. With a 75 or 100 foot setback - limiting up to 35' height is sufficient on those properties near residential or on smaller lots. A 35 foot tall building is still a significant height - especially on a smaller property like the corners in question. It's not "killing" development, but creating a transition, "feathering" back development with smaller buildings where appropriate and taller buildings where more property is available for buffering.

comment: I understand the proposed high density apartment development in North Orem that fits under the provisions of the State Street Master Plan. I have heard the neighbors are pushing back about the transition from the neighborhoods to the developments along state street and I believe this is a part of the Master Plan that was not fully considered. They are too abrupt and don’t make sense from a buffer perspective for state street either. These were some of issues raised when the master plan was adopted. How can they be acceptably addressed now so that we don’t have to have this type of issue every time a development occurs? The smaller parcels of property shouldn't have higher buildings on them anyways. If they are not large and are next to residentially zoned neighborhoods, then what's wrong with properties that cannot be developed.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I appreciate City Council member’s time and consideration on this matter. As a homeowner in the North Village District, I do not oppose the development of high-density housing that is in alignment with the ORIGINAL vision that was presented to us with appropriate access points and vibrant developments on State Street. The original vision looked great on paper but I believe this is the perfect time to reconsider its execution before it creates a greater problem in this area. We ask that you recognize that the desire of ONE developer to squeeze every last inch out of this landlocked property without proper infrastructure and access points would have a detrimental impact on thousands of property owners who live in the North Orem neighborhoods and those that drive through these intersections and not just those who live along 400 West. I agree with the proposal shared by Stephanie Visnaw and LaNeah Millet of increasing setbacks to 75 ft or even 100 ft from homeowners property lines with a 0-50 feet – zone identified as a “non- structure” area behind homes for the following reasons: NVD Edge zones do NOT have maximum height restrictions. Pictures were shared with City council members what potentially a 70 ft. building like Midtown 360 could look like from 50 ft. and 70 ft. views.Buildings can be built within that first 50 feet, just cannot exceed 35 feet. A 6 stories building 50ft away, starting at 35 ft. so close to homes it NOT protecting howmeowners and neighborhoods. It is extremely intrusive to homeowners living west and east of 400 West. The proposed 50-foot setback is NOT 50 feet of vacant, open land. A 0-50 feet – zone identified as a “non-structure” area behind homes with a 75 ft or 100 ft. would still allows for the development of the property with a parking lot, open space, and easement placement. City Planners would argue that our requests are more restrictive in nature, and the Mayor has said and I quote “if homeowners along 400 W. are against it then they should not have stayed”. I find this type of statement coming from our Mayor quite disheartening when some of these residents have lived along this street for generations! I would remind you when original plans of NVD were presented we were reassured by city planners that any large high density developments would remain on State Street and not engulf residential homes. NVD zone is different than other State street developments and setbacks must be addressed differently. It is closer to residential, smaller in size, and less commercial. This intersection is one of the most dangerous in Utah County (See Daily Herald, 2019), and 400 West is heavily trafficked. It’s important to highlight that the only ingress/ egress to this property is via only right turn onto 1600 N. No one is using the turnaround next to Quick quack to turn back westbound on 1600 N or to enter this property instead drivers use 400 West to make Uturns. Now, imagine the undrivable conditions a development so close to this intersection would create at this location We request that City Council considers appropriate setbacks to protect residential homes, and adequate access points to State Street to mitigate dangerous traffic conditions at this node. We fear that, if an increase of setbacks and limitations on height so close to homes is not granted, it will have a detrimental impact not only in this area but in other areas around our city where large developments are already taking place encroaching on residential areas and jeopardizing the safety of families in the neighborhoods and the preservation of the city we love.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I have read the response from Mayor Brunst to a neighbor. I hope each of you will read what the Mayor has to say about the proposed (and heavily contested) development at 1600 N and 400 W. What he said to this resident is what he is saying to each of us, who are also residents directly affected by the proposed development: • He claims the complex is “for condominiums to be sold and not for apartments … with 20 percent of affordable housing unit” [contained therein] o Selling a condo means absolutely NOTHING about it being occupied by the actual owner. Condos are bought as investment properties all the time, and then leased to occupants, the same as apartments. Being a condo doesn’t change a thing about its transitory nature within the community. Young families are not likely to have their starter home be in a high-rise condo. They find smaller/starter homes and townhomes in neighborhoods with parks, open spaces, other young families, newer amenities. This argument for helping young families build equity is false. o Putting in high-density and affordable housing within a stone’s throw of the State Liquor Store (some of the proposed property actually shares the parking lot with the State Liquor Store) is a BAD idea. We have repeatedly asked for studies about crime rates within close proximity of highdensity/affordable housing and the State Liquor Store, and still NOTHING has been provided by the developer nor the City of Orem. Unacceptable. o Orem City is already 40% rentals. FORTY PERCENT! • From Brunst directly: “I would ask you to consider what is reasonable – what if you were the other property owner – how would you want to be treated – what if you owned multiple homes on 400 West how would you want to be treated – have not all resudential (sp) homeowners known that they bordered commercial property along their back fence which would develop – and in fact if they are against this THEN THEY SHOULD NOT HAVE STAYED – we need to have fair property rights for all property owners … I believe that proper and fair compromises have been made – I would hope [you] would stop and consider what is fair for both sides equally.” (emphasis added) o This is NOT the language a Mayor should ever have, not privately and not to a resident being affected. How condescending, how insulting, how disgusting! This is spoken from a rich person living in CherApple about a rich developer living in the WordPerfect mansion community, ABOUT A NEIGHBORHOOD AND HOMEOWNERS THAT THEY ARE NOT PART OF. The audacity and insensitivity of a community leader to place ONE developer above what over 75+ families in just my immediate neighborhood have written and expressed discontent with. This should outrage everyone!!! There is no other way to say it. And for a rich person to simply suggest that a longtime resident of a neighborhood should just move away is appalling. Oh to have the financial freedom to do such a thing – only a rich person from CherApple could go so far. Oh to have the emotional lacking to simply leave friends and residents that we raise(d) our children with and mourned lost friends with because we see an undesirable circumstance arise. We residents have the right to defend our neighborhoods. The Mayor is supposed to stand up for our communities. He is supposed to lead out for all. Mayor Brunst’s words hold no compassion, no real desire for anything mutually beneficial. Give it up lessers, that’s what he’s asking. o I want an explanation from the Mayor about his choice of language, and also his relationship with the developer. He is saying, “I’m placing the rights of this one particular person over the rights of many, many others.” If the developer and the Mayor believe this project is so beneficial, then they can work to get this done in the neighborhoods they live in. (cue the outrage of the rich, safety-centered neighbors in CherApple and WordPerfect Park) The hypocrisy of the Mayor asking residents about their property rights of where they live versus the developer’s property rights of an investment property is breathtaking! o What compromises is the Mayor referring to? What has been offered for residents in this neighborhood? There aren't even sidewalks or gutter or lighting along some parts of 400 West. There are parts of an irrigation canal that have been open and unkempt FOR YEARS. What compromises have been made when basic street elements haven’t been provided? Is the Mayor receiving compromises personally? What consideration is he asking us to give up for things to be “fair for both sides equally” because having our traffic increase, our views ruined by 6-story buildings and potential increase in crime and property taxes seems like too much? What consideration has the developer given up to be “fair for both sides equally”? Seems quite unequal. I share the following from personal experience: • As a scout leader for Webelos Pack 876, we visited with Mayor Brunst on June 7, 2016. Our group asked the Mayor what the biggest energy problem facing Orem was (required question for the badge we were working on). Mayor Brunst responded that the Orem City Center offices and adjoining Library were the worst energy problem facing Orem. The office building had had “several” electrical fires, was not seismically sound, was not energy efficient. He laughingly called the building, “a bit of a tinderbox.” Our scouts discussed ways to fix the problem at meetings throughout the year. The following year we revisited the Mayor and asked the same question, hoping some new information could be shared about things being done to remedy the problem. Instead he changed the subject and talked about Orem water. I watched for information from the city for years, wondering when/if voting on bonds would come up. Nothing. When I saw the construction crews begin expansion of the new wing of the Orem City Offices and Library, I was physically sick. Why would anyone approve building a multi-million dollar facility onto an outdated “tinderbox”?! It defies fiscal responsibility and physical safety principles. • At the same meeting the Mayor said his favorite days as Mayor were groundbreaking ceremonies. Not opening new schools, not a student winning a state or national award, not safety and/or energy-efficient strides in government facilities, not improved family circumstances for all residents. No, this is a person who is out for himself and developers. This man is a not out for the good of the residents of Orem. We are a loooooong way from the “Most Livable City” status that Orem once boasted of.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I want to express my appreciation for the passion of Jason and Ryan as well as other city staff in working so hard to provide equitable solutions for all property owners - residential, commercial, or mixed use. I want to state that I am NOT against development of the state street corridor and I am NOT against growth and progress in our beautiful city. I just do not want it directly located in my backyard destroying the desirable Orem neighborhood residential feel. As a resident in the buffer zone on 400 West above 1600 North, I have a home and I want my property to be residential. Any buffer that limits the distance and elevation between me and commercial properties is extremely appreciated, the more the better. I do not want a developer to be able to build a skyrise next to my backyard. I would favor designs that support parking or common park uses to help buffer my home from tall development, also pushing tall buildings toward state street helps develop big & beautiful building fronts on state street where they are very ugly on my back yard property line. Additionally, I have huge concerns about traffic, parking, and access to a bottle necked property where large developments are being proposed. I trust that such a proposal would go through a good vetting process taking these concerns into consideration.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: Our neighborhood is asking you to create an ordinance that would provide a transition or buffer zone between our neighborhoods and high-rise/high density housing planned along State Street. We firmly believe that the intent of the State Street Master Plan is to place high-rise housing adjacent to State Street, and not along our back fence lines. As landscaping and parking will be required for any project built, we request you simply designate that the parking and landscaping required for such buildings should be located on the side of the development that abuts the homes—designate that area a non-structure. A nonstructure area would not impact the property rights of the commercial landowners. A good example is the Alpine Credit Union building. ACU placed the parking for their building behind the buildings and adjacent to the homes, thus creating a buffer. Parking and open green space will be a part of any commercial or residential development built in Orem. This isn’t an issue of limiting property use, just directing it. We affirm that the Districts were established to pull high-density housing out of single-family neighborhoods. We could reword that to say, the intent is to put high-density housing on State Street and the intent is to mitigate the impact of high-density housing on single-family homes. Our proposal of a wider, 100-foot setback fits within both of the objectives of mitigating impact, while still allowing business owners to develop their land. Property rights on both sides are being affected here. We feel our proposal of combining a setback, along with non-structure area guidelines, is a good balance for all property owners. Thank you for your efforts to understand this issue and I hope you will institute ordinances that will give builders the guidelines to create their projects in a way that will protect the property rights of the homeowners.
